Une femme aujourd’hui

Un film de Robert Guédiguian

Avec Marilou Aussilloux, Ariane Ascaride, Jean-Pierre Darroussin, Grégoire Leprince-Ringuet, Gérard Meylan, Lola Naymark

Genre :

Durée : 2h03

Note : Si le téléchargement ne fonctionne pas en cliquant directement sur un lien, veuillez cliquer avec le bouton droit sur ce lien et choisir l'option "Enregistrer la cible du lien sous..." ou "Enregistrer le lien sous..." ou "Télécharger le fichier lié sous..." suivant votre navigateur.

Juliette, 30 ans, semble avoir tout pour elle : un poste prestigieux dans la finance, une belle maison, une vie rythmée par les voyages et les amours de passage. Lorsqu’elle est agressée par un collègue, son monde s’effondre. Juliette s'engage alors sur un nouveau chemin pour redonner un sens à sa vie.

article_text:
Elizabeth Banks has given two thumbs to “ The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping .”

“I’ve seen the film, and it’s amazing,” Banks, who played Effie Trinket in the first four movies of the “Hunger Games” franchise from 2012-2015, told me Wednesday night at the Airbnb.org Gala in Los Angeles.

Based on Suzanne Collins’ 2025 novel “Sunrise on the Reaping,” the new movie centers on a young Haymitch ( Joseph Zada , taking over the role from Woody Harrelson) as he fights to survive while competing in the 50th Hunger Games. The cast also features Jesse Plemons as Plutarch, Ralph Fiennes as President Snow, Kieran Culkin as Caesar Flickerman, Elle Fanning as Effie Trinket, Maya Hawke as Wiress and Kelvin Harrison Jr. as Beetee. New characters in the film franchise are played by the likes of Mckenna Grace, Glenn Close and Whitney Peak, among others.

'Nobody Wants This' Season 3 Opens With 6.2 Million Views in Four Days

Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson and Woody Harrelson return as Katniss, Peeta and Haymitch in a flash-forward scene.

“Joseph is a perfect Woody Harrelson,” Banks said. “He’s fantastic. I can’t wait for people to see it.”

Original "Hunger Games" star Elizabeth Banks has seen "Sunrise on the Reaping." Here's what she told me last night about the latest installment of the franchise. https://t.co/IVQHSKIXQH @variety #justforvariety #redcarpet pic.twitter.com/eKTWoIUk3y — Marc Malkin (@marcmalkin) October 29, 2026

Earlier this month, I talked to Zada about his work on the movie. His first day filming took place on the Cornucopia. “You’re sitting there and there are 47 other kids around, and there’s a this massive drone, so there’s no crew,” he said. “It was the most mental place to film. Getting ready to run into it, I had all those nerves and it worked out for the character.”

He recalled sharing scenes with Plemons. “He’s so good, and once you get into a little bit, he’s so easy to play with that you really feel like you’re on fire in the moment.”

Close proved to be a jokester at times. “She would growl at me,” Zada said, laughing. “She was so lovely all the time, [but] she’d flip into the character and she’d look at you and hiss. You’re just startled. Just for fun, just to mess with people, I guess.”

Just for fun, just to mess with… pic.twitter.com/4mvy715QaM — Marc Malkin (@marcmalkin) October 29, 2026

He added, “She’s the most wonderful person ever, so generous outside of acting as well. Just always wanted to come up to me and talk and see how I was doing. She’s gorgeous.”

“The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” opens in theaters Nov. 20 from Lionsgate.

editorial_title_zh: 乌苏拉·冯·里丁斯瓦德，巨型雪松雕塑家，逝世，享年84岁
editorial_excerpt_zh: 她以兼具人性触感的雕塑回应了极简主义的苦行风格。

Rydingsvard", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/ursula-von-rydingsvard/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "冯·里丁斯瓦德经常使用4×4的雪松木方，雕刻出似乎在起伏和变幻的高耸形态。由有机材料制成的它们，有时甚至看起来宛如生命体，在空中盘旋，就像移动中的神秘动物。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当冯·里丁斯瓦德在20世纪70年代中期开始使用雪松时，极简主义是纽约的主导风格，为了获得关注，雕塑家们常常将钢材和其他金属焊接成高耸于观众之上的宏伟壮观造型。冯·里丁斯瓦德对这种风格注重理论的方法及其冰冷的情调感到烦恼。“这里面没有性感，甚至没有任何人性，”她曾对策展人马克·罗森塔尔（Mark Rosenthal）说道，后者于2018年在费城的织物工作坊与博物馆（Fabric Workshop and Museum）为她举办了一场作品展。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "冯·里丁斯瓦德也学会了焊接，但这种方法“比想象的还要令人沮丧”，她曾对评论家杰森·法拉戈（Jason Farago）这样说。不过，她找到了一个令自己满意的解决方法：她将焊枪贴近一块钢板，当焊枪接触表面时形成一个小液滴。“热度以一种美丽、精致的方式让钢板呈现出有机感，”她说，“这一点我喜欢。”", "links": [{"text": "told the critic Jason Farago", "url": "https://evenmagazine.com/ursula-von-rydingsvard/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "冯·里丁斯瓦德是通过画家迈克尔·穆尔赫ン（Michael Mulhern）接触到雪松的，后者为她购买了许多4x4木方。随后，她将这些木头带到金属加工工作室并将其切开，沉浸于她如何能够获得“感觉像大地，或感觉像是有血有肉”的形态之中，正如她所说的那样。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "正如评论家雷切尔·韦茨勒（Rachel Wetzler）于2018年在《美国艺术》（Art in America）中写道：“木材的标准化规格中和了她雕塑的原始特质，这些雕塑隐约让人联想到化石、岩石峡谷或汹涌的波浪等事物；她最优秀的作品往往善于利用堆叠木材底层网格结构与她发掘出的参差不齐、不规则形态之间充满活力的张力。”", "links": [{"text": "wrote in Art in America", "url": "她经常澄清，树干是行不通的——她的材料必须是4x4的雪松木方。她给出的理由是树干保留自身形态的程度太高了。关于4x4木方，她曾说：“这些是中性的。它们对你没有任何要求。它们就像一张白纸。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "冯·里丁斯瓦德的材料库后来扩展到了丝绸、毛发和牛肠，她将这些材料优雅地雕刻成大型物件，尽管体量庞大，却从不显得盛气凌人。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在她的艺术中，一些评论家看到了对冯·里丁斯瓦德生平经历的呼应。例如，她最著名的作品之一《扎科帕内》（Zakopane，1987），其上方带有尖刺突起，下方则是成袋的木质结构。作品的标题指的是冯·里丁斯瓦德母亲出生的波兰城镇。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "但冯·里丁斯瓦德坚称，她的作品与她的亲身经历仅仅是隐性相关的。“我有一种感觉，我和一个我从未经历过的过去有着强烈的联系，那就是农民的过去，”她对法拉戈说道，“并不是说我想去经历它；我从未要求过它。但它某种程度上就在我的血液里流淌，不管我愿不愿意。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "ARTnews", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "乌苏拉·冯·里丁斯瓦德于1942年出生在德国代森（Deensen）。她的母亲是波兰人，父亲是乌克兰人；两人都是农民。纳粹征召了她的父亲，强迫他在劳工营工作。战争结束后，她和家人被安置在德国的一个流离失所者营地中。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "1950年，全家搬到了康涅狄格州普兰维尔（Plainville），她的母亲在那里的一家餐馆工作，父亲则在一家工厂找到了一份工作，同时还帮忙照看邻近的一个农场。她的生活有着鲜明的蓝领阶层印记，她后来回忆说，在普兰维尔，“根本没有‘艺术家’这种东西”。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "最终，冯·里丁斯瓦德也在她母亲工作的餐馆找了一份工作。她后来就读于新罕布什尔大学（University of New Hampshire）和迈阿密大学珊瑚盖布尔斯分校（University of Miami, Coral Gables），并分别获得了学士和硕士学位。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "她最终和第一任丈夫弥尔顿·冯·里丁斯瓦德（Milton von Rydingsvard）一起搬到了加利福尼亚州奥克兰，两人育有一女乌苏拉·安妮·冯·里丁斯瓦德（Ursula Anne von Rydingsvard）。她在1973年与他离婚，随后带着女儿前往纽约，并立即入读哥伦比亚大学的艺术项目。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "冯·里丁斯瓦德在艰难困苦的条件下继续谋生。她靠食品券度日，并在哈莱姆区的125街租了一间公寓，她形容当时那里“很危险”。但她也发现，在30出头的年纪成为单亲母亲是一段充满解放感的经历。终于，她可以做自己想做的事了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "通过哥伦比亚大学，她得以初窥纽约艺术界的面貌。她热切地聆听评论家马克斯·科佐夫（Max Kozloff）关于马塞尔·杜尚（Marcel Duchamp）的讲座。她还师从艺术史学家迈耶·夏皮罗（Meyer Schapiro）和艺术家乔治·苏加曼（George Sugarman）。随后，在1975年毕业后，她在苏荷区（SoHo）买了一间阁楼并设立了工作室。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "1981年，她迁往布鲁克林，并在那里度过了其余的艺术生涯。1985年，她与神经科学家保罗·格林加德（Paul Greengard）结婚，后者于2019年逝世。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "她的雕塑作品得到了广泛展出，场地从纽约州北部的斯托姆金艺术中心（Storm King Art Center）到英国的约克郡雕塑公园（Yorkshire Sculpture Park）不等。随着获得更多的曝光，冯·里丁斯瓦德的野心也不断扩大，使她能够承接规模更大的委托创作。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": Ursula von Rydingsvard , a sculptor who responded to the austerity of Minimalism with monumental cedar sculptures that had a distinctly human touch, died in New York on Tuesday following a battle with Alzheimer’s disease. She was 84, according to the New York Times .

Frequently using 4×4 cedar beams, von Rydingsvard crafted towering forms that appear to undulate and shift. Made of organic material, they at times even looked as though they were alive, spinning through the air like mysterious animals on the move.

When von Rydingsvard began working with cedar in the mid-1970s, Minimalism was the dominant style in New York, and in order to gain attention, sculptors often welded steel and other metals into imposing, grand forms that loomed high above viewers. Von Rydingsvard chafed against the style’s theory-driven approach and its cold sensibility. “There was no sexiness, and there wasn’t even any humanity,” she once told the curator Mark Rosenthal, who organized a 2018 show of her work at the Fabric Workshop and Museum in Philadelphia.

Von Rydingsvard, too, learned to weld, but the method was “more frustrating than imaginable,” as she once told the critic Jason Farago . Yet she found a solution that pleased her: She applied a hot rod to a sheet of steel, allowing it to create a droplet when it met the surface. “The heat made the sheet organic in a beautiful, delicate way,” she said. “That I liked.”

Cedar came to von Rydingsvard through the painter Michael Mulhern, who purchased many 4x4s for her. She then took the wood to a metalworking studio and proceeded to slice through it, delighting in the ways that she could obtain “forms that felt like the earth, or felt fleshy,” as she put it.

As critic Rachel Wetzler wrote in Art in America in 2018, “The wood’s standardized format offsets the primordial qualities of her sculptures, which loosely suggest, among other things, fossils, rocky canyons, or cresting waves; her best works tend to exploit the animating tension between the underlying gridded structure of the stacked wood and the ragged, irregular forms she unearths.”

Tree trunks were a no go, she often clarified—her material had to be cedar 4x4s. Her stated reason was that tree trunks retain their form too well. Of the 4x4s, she said, “These are neutral. They don’t ask anything of you. They’re like a blank piece of paper.”

Von Rydingsvard’s arsenal of materials came to include silk, hair, and cow intestines, all of which she elegantly sculpted into large-scale objects that never felt domineering, even despite their size.

In her art, some critics saw references to von Rydingsvard’s biography. For example, Zakopane (1987), one of her most famous works, features sacs of wood beneath spiky protrusions above. The work’s title refers to the Polish town where von Rydingsvard’s mother was born.

But von Rydingsvard insisted that her work was only implicitly related to her lived experience. “I have this feeling that I have this strong link to a past that I never experienced, the peasant farmer past,” she told Farago. “Not that I want to experience it; I never asked for it. But it sort of runs through my blood, whether I want it or not.”

Ursula von Rydingsvard was born in 1942 in Deensen, Germany. Her mother was Polish and her father was Ukrainian; both were peasant farmers. The Nazis conscripted her father and forced him to work at a labor camp. Once the war ended, she and her family were placed in a displaced persons camp in Germany.

In 1950, the family moved to Plainville, Connecticut, where her mother worked at a restaurant and her father took a job at a factory while also helping man an adjacent farm. Hers was a distinctly blue-collar existence, and she would later recall that, in Plainville, there was “no such thing as an artist.”

Eventually, von Rydingsvard also took a job at her mother’s restaurant. She later studied at the University of New Hampshire and the University of Miami, Coral Gables, where she respectively received her bachelor’s and master’s degrees.

She eventually moved to Oakland, California, with her first husband, Milton von Rydingsvard, with whom she had a daughter, Ursula Anne von Rydingsvard. She divorced him in 1973, then set off to New York with her, promptly enrolling at Columbia University’s art program.

Von Rydingsvard continued to survive under hardscrabble conditions. She lived off food stamps, and she rented an apartment on 125th Street in Harlem, which she described as “dangerous” at the time. But she also found being a single mother at in her early 30s to be a liberating experience. Finally, she could do what she wanted.

Through Columbia, she got a taste of New York’s art world. She eagerly listened to the critic Max Kozloff lecturing on Marcel Duchamp. She also studied with art historian Meyer Schapiro and artist George Sugarman. Then, after graduating in 1975, she purchased a loft in SoHo and set up a studio.

In 1981, she decamped for Brooklyn, where she remained for the rest of her career. In 1985, she married the neuroscientist Paul Greengard, who died in 2019.

Her sculptures have been shown widely, in venues ranging from the Storm King Art Center in Upstate New York to the Yorkshire Sculpture Park in England. As they received greater exposure, von Rydingsvard’s ambitions expanded, allowing her to tackle ever larger commissions.

In 2013, she premiered Ona (2013), a rippling array of cedar blocks that can still be found beneath the oculus of Brooklyn’s Barclay Center. Weighing in at 12,000 pounds and standing 19 feet tall, it has a title that translates from the Polish for “she” or “her.” She welcomed the possibility that one could easily caress her sculpture.

“I would actually love people to touch it,” she told the New York Times upon Ona ’s debut. “The acid from fingers polishes it, like the Buddhas getting their bellies rubbed.”

But she also expressed reservations about the improper preservation of her work, which she wanted to feel permanent and immovable. She told Farago, “I don’t want my work to rot. Even after I’m gone.”

SPOILERS: This post contains details about Peacock ‘s Crystal Lake

As Crystal Lake brings Jason Voorhees fans to his roots, the Peacock prequel series takes the Friday the 13th franchise back to where it all began.

Series creator Brad Caleb Kane told Deadline “the amazing thing” about filming the eight-episode show — all episodes now available to stream — where the original 1980 slasher also filmed in Blairstown, NJ, is that the township “hasn’t changed in 45 years.”

“It’s still exactly the same,” explained Kane. “The structures are the same, maybe some paint jobs are different, and we had to do a little bit of that. But basically, it’s exactly the same town intact as it was 45 years ago, which is amazing.”

Fans of the original Sean S. Cunningham-helmed horror film might remember one of the opening scenes, in which camp counselor Annie Phillips (Robbi Morgan) hitchhikes through Crystal Lake, crossing a small bridge and cutting a corner in downtown Blairstown with a noticeable round red payphone on the sidewalk and visiting Trudy’s diner before meeting her demise.

Watch on Deadline

In episode 4, “A New Beginning,” writers Evan Endicott and Josh Stoddard re-created the scene with a hitchhiking hippy named Willow (Oona Roche), even rebuilding the interior of Trudy’s diner on a soundstage.

Kane also emphasized the importance of filming in New Jersey, “because honestly, like trees look different in Jersey. You can’t re-create that feel anywhere else, so we wanted to re-create that feel and the only way to do it is in the same state.”

Although the nearby Camp No-Be-Bo-Sco, which is still an active camp and horror fan destination, was not available to stand in for Camp Crystal Lake as it once did in 1980, Kane and directors Celine Held and Logan George were able to rebuild the camp’s boathouse on a soundstage in order to “faithfully” re-create movie’s opening kill with his own twist in episode 5, “The New Blood”.

“It’s still there and it’s still intact, and we walked through it, because we couldn’t shoot there,” explained Kane. “And obviously now that you’ve seen the show, you know that we re-create a scene in that boathouse, shot-for-shot from the movie. Our great production designer Lester Cohen rebuilt it from scratch to the exact specifications at Camp Ocawasin in New Jersey, which was our campground that we created for the show.”

In addition to re-creating some memorable scenes and locations in the series about Jason Voorhees’ grieving mother Pam (Linda Cardellini), Crystal Lake also revisits some fan-favorite locals from screenwriter Victor Miller’s slasher in its cast of characters, including diner owner Trudy (played by Dorothy Kobs in the first movie, Bernadette Quigley in the prequel series), police officer Dorf (Ron Millke, Cameron Scoggins) and hermit Crazy Ralph (Walt Gorney, Nick Cordileone), as well as new faces, including Pam’s romantic interest, Officer Levon Brooks (William Catlett), his reporter sister Brianna (Devin Kessler) and Pam’s single friend Rita (Joy Suprano).

Kane found it “exciting” revisiting Crystal Lake and its residents through the series, which he envisions through a “Twin Peaks-y vibe.”

“I mean, this is a world that I return to over and over and over again,” he said. “I return to these movies, we all do, somehow. They became iconic for a reason. But there’s a lot we don’t know about the town. We meet these really colorful characters in the first movie, we meet Trudy and Officer Dorf and so-called Crazy Ralph, even though he turns out to have a point. But we don’t see that much of them ultimately. Some are dispatched, some are just there for momentary common comic relief.”

Kane continued, “And, you know, with a show like this, we have the opportunity to open it up and spend a little more time with them. Everybody loves a small-town show, and within the world of Friday the 13th , that just becomes more amplified and interesting.”

With a wealth of characters to explore (and eventually slaughter), Kane hopes to revisit Crystal Lake for another season. “I do have ideas for Season 2 in mind,” he confirmed.

“Obviously, it’s not just Pam’s story, it’s Crystal Lake, so you have all of the peripheral characters who are interesting to me,” explained Kane. “You have the opportunity for this to be more of a Twin Peaks -y kind of vibe, with Ralph and with Dorf and Trudy and all of those characters. There’s a lot more to get into with them. But obviously, the nexus is always gonna be Pam and Jason and their story.”

After giving fans “a little dopamine hit” with his nods to the original movie, Kane noted that the show “could run into the events” of Friday the 13th (1980) if Peacock gives them enough time.

“It wouldn’t happen in a second season,” Kane clarified. “There’s more story to tell, for the residents of Crystal Lake and to the extent that Linda wants to continue the journey with us, with Pam. So, we’ll see.”

As for Cardellini, she joked that she’s game to continue the show until Pam “kills every resident” of Crystal Lake.

article_text:
Dubbed the “Opera House of western Sydney”, Powerhouse Parramatta’s white lattice exoskeleton, composed from 1,300 individual pieces and wrapping 30,000 sq metres of interior space, has already become a familiar landmark.

Even better known, perhaps, is the project’s controversial history . Since the Parramatta outpost was announced in 2014, a vocal group of dissenters led by former staff and trustees has lamented what they see as the neglect of the museum’s Ultimo site in favour of a new infrastructure project, and what they say is a shift away from the museum’s core business towards contemporary art and events.

The eye-watering price tag – $915m, in an era of funding precarity for the arts – has also come under scrutiny, culminating in a New South Wales Treasury investigation into allegations over the museum’s governance and procurement practices. In late August, 10 weeks from the scheduled opening, CEO Lisa Havilah was stood down while the investigation unfolded.

When the major new venue opens to the public on Saturday, the big question will be: was it worth it? What will it bring to Parramatta – and will it be enough to bring the rest of Sydney, and the rest of Australia, out west?

Powerhouse is sweetening the pot with a 23-day opening festival of performances, parties, talks, screenings and workshops, with 65% of the program free. When Guardian Australia visited last week, the space was crowded with installation crew in hi-vis, hard hats and steel-capped boots. But even with its exhibitions in various states of readiness, it was hard not to be dazzled.

Dizzying spectacles and a sense of calm

The steel exoskeleton that has been such a prominent addition to Parramatta’s skyline is more than decorative. Encasing two towers, and built from 12,000 tonnes of steel, it’s what allows the building to boast massive column-free exhibition spaces up to 18m in height, including the largest in Australia.

But at first encounter, perhaps the most striking thing about the Moreau Kusunoki and Genton-designed building is the sense of calm it evokes. This is a building that is constantly calling you to slow down, take a breath and look beyond its architecture to the city, landscape and Parramatta River below.

The glass facade and abundance of natural light is complemented by an airy colour palette, all creams, white and light greys – including interior walls covered in a pale, textured render made from 600,000 crushed oyster shells, locally and sustainably sourced. Wide corridors flanking the exhibition spaces are lined with chairs and lounges that invite you to pause and take in the view.

This peace is particularly necessary given the dizzying spectacles of Powerhouse Parramatta’s five opening exhibitions – including a tribute to space and flight; a celebration of the shopping mall; a kids’ exhibition themed around the dark; and a showcase of British designer Es Devlin – which otherwise risk sensory overload.

Coups de théâtre abound: secret doorways and dramatic reveals; a mirror maze; a copse of Christmas firs; a massive replica meteorite taking up an entire exhibition space. There’s a recreation of the historic Roselands shopping mall fountain; a restored 1920s elevator transporting visitors with access needs between exhibition floors; and a rainbow-hued walk-in installation by American light artist James Turrell at the top of a tower.

Throughout the spaces, museum objects (more than 1,600 from the 500,000-strong collection, supplemented by around as many loans) jostle with commissioned artworks, lavishly designed displays and interactive exhibits. The exhibitions are fuelled by wonder, spectacle and nostalgia – and are hard to resist.

Planes, engines, rockets – and a James Turrell

Task Eternal is Powerhouse Parramatta’s flagship opening exhibition – and the only one that adults will have to pay an entry fee for ($30/$20 concession; 16 and unders get in free). A celebration of flight and space travel, it takes over the museum’s main hall: 2,000 sq metres with 18-metre-high ceilings, bringing together objects from the Powerhouse collection as well as loans, commissions and literary texts – including excerpts from US science fiction author Ted Chiang , whose short story Tower of Babylon inspired the exhibition’s structure, including a zigzagging tower which visitors ascend and descend.

Hero items include delicate sketches by Leonardo da Vinci; a bumarang (boomerang) – an example of ingenious Indigenous aerodynamic design – collected from Burramatta/Parramatta in the early 19th century; a “boilerplate” (or testing model) Apollo command module from the 1960s; and the spacesuit worn by Leonard Nimoy’s Spock in Star Trek.

Aircraft from different eras, including the 19th-century flying rigs of Australian aviation pioneer Lawrence Hargrave, take pride of place. There is an entire room full of engines, and lots of rockets too, including a Skylark research rocket deployed at Woomera in the 70s, and a fully functional retro Rocket Playground from the 1960s.

Among the many stunning artworks, the star exhibit – at the top of the tower structure – is a perception-testing “ganzfeld” installation by US light artist James Turrell, accessible for those who bought a special Turrell-inclusive ticket ($40 for adults, $10 for kids). Eight viewers at a time are invited into a room with curved walls and a shifting cycle of coloured light, which induces the kind of disorientation experienced by pilots in certain altitudes and atmospheres.

Task Eternal is overwhelming in its scope and visual magnificence. It’s also a little discombobulating. Rather than chronology, it is structured around four “acts” exploring not only the history and technology of air and space travel, but our “cultural relationship with the sky” and “the human compulsion to ascend, leave Earth and return”. It flits between eras, topics and modes of storytelling; between science, engineering, design and art.

It also works hard to shed the western, patriarchal and colonial narratives around space and flight, and to weave in lesser-known histories and perspectives, including First Nations technologies and cosmologies. This doesn’t make for a smooth, coherent journey; though time, attention to wall texts and repeat visits may yield the kind of rich experience it aims for.

A secret playground that’s sure to be a hit

The Mall , a tribute to the social, cultural and design history of shopping centres, was only partially installed a week ahead of opening, but looks to be similarly maximalist. The Dark , the Powerhouse’s exhibition for children aged 4 to 12 set in a massive replica meteorite more than 22m long, will be an absolute hit – and not just because it’s top secret: no photographs are allowed, and visitors will have to bag their smartphones before entering.

We are allowed to describe how it works though: visitors enter via a dark, narrow tunnel followed by a series of glowing chambers, lined and stuffed with more than 800 objects, including sparkling minerals, retro toys, ancient artefacts and modern treasures (including the first item the museum collected, in 1882: a jar of peas ). Part playground, part discovery trail, items are arranged from toddler to adult height, and there are enough hidden delights and nostalgic treats to thaw the most frosty heart – including animations drawing on First Nations creation stories, and the museum’s most Googled object: a heart-emblazoned shirt worn by Leonardo DiCaprio in Baz Luhrmann’s Romeo + Juliet . There’s not much narrative here, and some might grumble that it is light on science and learning, but museums desperately need to attract young audiences – and this might do the trick.

The calmest of the opening exhibits, titled Overflow, is an installation on the eastern building’s third floor: a 16-metre high-definition LED display of short films by director Ivan Sen, featuring breathtaking footage, each spotlighting one of seven Indigenous organisations from NSW who care for water, country and community.

In front of the screen is a shallow pool with water that laps with the tides of the river. Visitors are encouraged to take their shoes off and get their feet wet; there’s a sensorial magic about being 30m high, with your feet in the water and the sky on either side of you.

“We’re on a flood plain,” says Beau James, director of First Nations for the Powerhouse, gesturing to the Parramatta River out the window. In fact the location of the building was its own controversy for that very reason . “That river has always ebbed and flowed, that’s its natural way of moving. We wanted to honour water.”

As part of the commission, the museum invested an undisclosed amount of money in the organisations featured in Sen’s films. “We asked them: ‘What’s something you’ve always really wanted to do but have never been able to get funds for?’” says James.

The funded proposals include tagging marine life in Gamay (Botany Bay); clearing rubbish and mitigating pollution in the Parramatta River; and an initiative for clearing invasive European carp from the Barwon River in Brewarrina.

Es Devlin’s Australian debut

The final exhibition brings together recent works by British designer Es Devlin whose peripatetic career has encompassed theatre, fashion, public art and arena concerts (she has designed tours for Beyoncé, U2 and Lady Gaga, as well as Olympic ceremonies and Super Bowl half-time shows).

But Powerhouse’s exhibition – her Australian debut – sees Devlin in a more poetic and philosophical mode. Made over the last decade (and adjusted here for their Australian debuts), the five works, spread across four main rooms, represent Devlin’s attempts to use participatory art and interactive design to induce shifts of awareness and perspective; and to help rewire our sense of connection to the living world and each other.

The visual highlight is a giant multi-floored mirror maze, which takes up 24m x 10.7m of floor space and is designed to represent the “arterial geometries of lungs and trees”. But the soul of the exhibition is the participatory work Collective Portrait: a room with a 24m table and an equally long, unspooling reel of white paper, with an invitation to sit down on either side of the table for 15 minutes and draw the person opposite you.

The point is not so much the drawing as the silent interpersonal exchange between strangers. “I’ve been practising this around the world, and I’ve found whoever I practise it with, it can be quietly transformational,” says Devlin.

She has also created a sixth, temporary work for the museum’s month-long opening festival: an Australian iteration of her 2022 outdoor work Come Home Again, featuring her own hand-drawn sketches of 244 endangered local species, and choral tributes which will be performed at dusk most nights through November within her illuminated outdoor installation on the Powerhouse’s riverside lawn.

“I’m hoping that if we set up the rhythm of these evensong moments over the opening days and weeks, that people will continue to gather here. That it’s like a beacon.”

Devlin, who has exhibited in the world’s top galleries and museums, describes Powerhouse Parramatta as a “magnificent” building with “astounding” opening exhibitions. “The fact that people are going to not just learn things but feel things and therefore remember what they learned? I think it’s going to make it a destination for people to come from far and wide.”

With the help of Jean Hutson and Regina Andrews, two librarians at the Schomburg Center of Research in Black Culture, he threw a cocktail party in Duke Ellington’s apartment, convening a joyful group of surviving Harlem Renaissance artists, writers, and musicians. That day, Greaves and four camera operators (including his son, David) filmed the conversations, recitations, and deliberations of Richard Bruce Nugent, Aaron Douglas, Eubie Banks, James Van Der Zee, and other luminaries in colorful 16mm film, capturing a once-in-a-lifetime moment that resembled life 50 years earlier."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "As Greaves began piecing the documentary together with David, he realized the still period photography he’d collected and the film they’d just shot didn’t match aesthetically. At least until 2022—eight years after Greaves died—when his widow, Louise Archambault Greaves, obtained a grant from the Ford Foundation to digitize and assemble the unfinished archive. article_text:
In 1972, legendary director William Greaves set out to record history. With the help of Jean Hutson and Regina Andrews, two librarians at the Schomburg Center of Research in Black Culture, he threw a cocktail party in Duke Ellington’s apartment, convening a joyful group of surviving Harlem Renaissance artists, writers, and musicians. That day, Greaves and four camera operators (including his son, David) filmed the conversations, recitations, and deliberations of Richard Bruce Nugent, Aaron Douglas, Eubie Banks, James Van Der Zee, and other luminaries in colorful 16mm film, capturing a once-in-a-lifetime moment that resembled life 50 years earlier.

As Greaves began piecing the documentary together with David, he realized the still period photography he’d collected and the film they’d just shot didn’t match aesthetically. Greaves eventually incorporated the stills into a 30-minute 1974 documentary From These Roots , but the live-action footage sat unused for decades. At least until 2022—eight years after Greaves died—when his widow, Louise Archambault Greaves, obtained a grant from the Ford Foundation to digitize and assemble the unfinished archive. Before Louise died a year later, she handed the project’s keys to David and his daughter, Liani Greaves, to complete the film with editor and producer Anne de Mare.

The result is Once Upon a Time In Harlem , a minor miracle—or, as New Yorker film critic Richard Brody wrote last year , “one of the greatest cinematic works of creative nonfiction” that he’s “ever seen.” Leaning into his father’s experimental style and double-screen formats (a nod to his masterwork Symbiopsychotaxiplasm ), David captures the bustling spirit of the apartment’s lively, candid figures, intermixing occasional talking heads and history with the handheld immediacy of their cross-room talk. Like his father intended, David pulls you into snippets of intimate discussion, then pivots as real-time interruptions funnel into larger group recollections. It feels like one living, breathing document, layering a 1920s community onto a 1970s landscape seen through today’s lens.

As Once Upon a Time in Harlem begins its theatrical run, I caught up with David Greaves inside NEON’s Manhattan office. In a thoughtful, at-times-emotional interview, he reflected on his memories working with his father, piecing together the archive, and learning more about that foundational era of Black life.

The Film Stage: When your dad started this documentary in 1972, you were a 26-year-old camera operator. You’re watching all these luminaries walk into Duke Ellington’s home. What do you remember about preparing for that day?

David Greaves: Well, that’s so funny. You’re the first person to ask me about preparing for that day, because that’s the part I remember. I don’t remember the day itself because I was working. When I saw myself and others in the rough cut, the outtakes, and in the mirrors, it’s like, “Oh, yeah, that’s right. That was me.” I remember my father telling me that I was going to be one of the camera people. And I knew this was a big deal. In preparation for that, I usually read a book called Family of Man . It was a family of images. And so I always go through that for framing and that kind of stuff. But the actual shoot itself: I cannot give you a moment.

How familiar were you with all of these people in the room? Did you know everyone by name and their backgrounds?

No, I only met two people. One was Richard B. Moore. He was a mentor to my father. I met him at his bookstore one time. And then, of course, Eubie Blake, because we did From These Roots , and Eubie did the music for it. It was incredible. What had happened was that I picked him up and brought him to the studio. And there was a heavy rock band there, heavy metal. So finally they finished and then we went in. And then Eubie walked over to the piano. And he’s 89 years old. And the little guys were like, “OK, watch this old guy.” And then Eubie sat down.

I’m sorry—I will tear up if I tell this. He sat down to play, and [my dad] said, “Eubie, the men are coming back from the war. Play it.” Eubie hit it. “Eubie, the people are migrating from the South.” Eubie hit it. “People are enjoying…” Eubie hit it. Those guys were like, “What the hell?” I mean, the whole atmosphere in the control room changed.

He knew every cue for what you wanted.

Dad just told him what to do, and he’d hit it. It was unbelievable! You had to be there to see that.

David and Liani Greaves at the 64th New York Film Festival. Photo by Sean DiSerio.

As you were filming Once Upon a Time , what was your relationship like with your dad and his filmmaking? Did you understand what he was trying to achieve with a lot of his films, or were you just kind of along for the ride?

I didn’t meet my father until I was 12. I first worked with him one Christmas break. I was finishing up The First World Festival of Negro Arts and I rolled up the outtakes of Symbiopsychotaxiplasm . He was telling me about the things he was doing. “Gee, that sounds more fun than spending another couple of years in the library.” So I said, “Yeah, let me go to Columbia instead of California for graduate school.” So I went to Columbia. I worked with him for, like, 15 years or so. They say in the film, “It is the now when you’re there.”

When we did Symbiopsychotaxiplasm: Take One , it got all these awards, and I just thought that if you do a film, you get awards. I just thought that was the way things worked, because Voice of La Raza , we got awards. The hallway was lined with awards. And so my father obviously was very good at it, and I was sitting next to him all the time, taking my notes and stuff. I guess he’s in my brain because, when I started to go back over this footage I said, “Oh, I want to go back and see something.” And my hand shot out to where the control panel would be on the editing machine some 50 years later. I realized that’s the same thing that was going on in my head in terms of being back in the editing room.

You mentioned the idea of not knowing when you’re “in an era” when you’re in the middle of it. Was that also the case for you as you filmed the cocktail party? Did you realize how special this would be at that moment?

Well, when I was preparing for it, I knew it was going to be special. I knew it was going to be a special time. But I did not know what it would be now. It was a film that we were doing…

You were expecting this to come out the following year.

Yeah, exactly. You’re working on the film now, and you don’t know what it’s gonna be 50 years later when people look at it. “Oh, Jesus, I had no idea that was happening.” I compare it to a story I was reading—they have a new telescope, the Nancy Grace Roman Telescope, which is more powerful than the Webb. It can see as close to the Big Bang as you can get—but it can’t see it itself. This film is like that. It brings you as close to the Harlem Renaissance as you can get. You can’t see it, but it’s as close as you can get. In the film, Richard B. Moore says, “Everything converged, and there was this little glow of light and learning.” And that’s what we’re looking at: the glow.

Your dad really struggled for decades with how to structure and format this footage into the movie he wanted. Why do you think he struggled with this so much?

He and my stepmother, Louise Archambault Greaves, wanted to show the effect of the Renaissance throughout the decades, because they were filming up to the early 2000s, shooting digitally at that point. So I think that’s what that was. But he never returned to say, “Let’s just do this .” He did an original rough cut, but he didn’t go beyond that. And I don’t know; I can’t give you a thinking of why he chose not to just complete it with the footage we had. But his treatments involved some contemporary talking heads—Sidney Poitier, Brock Peters doing narrations and stuff. So we decided to just stay with that time. And that worked out.

This entire restoration started with Louise receiving a Ford Foundation grant in 2022. How did you become involved with completing it after that?

After she got the grant, the film and the footage were restored. And then she passed. The footage was completed and the restoration was completed. The first meeting, I remember, we had at Bill Bland’s office, who did the restoration, and I said, “I’m not just gonna turn it over to an editor.” But it was when we were up at Firelight Studio with Stanley Nelson and Marcia Smith when Marcia said, “OK, so who’s gonna direct this?” I said, “I will.” I couldn’t imagine turning it over to anybody else.

It felt personal to you.

Sure. I couldn’t see anybody else doing this. And Louise and I had spoken about it. She would say, “We’re gonna get you a director. What about so-and-so?” Well, he didn’t know Bill. “What about so-and-so?” I was quiet during all her discussions. I just kept my mouth shut. She couldn’t make that final decision. And she gave a note to me. She said, “At the end, y’all will do it.” So, in the end, that’s how it came.

At the start of this project, how did you start thinking about what to highlight in 60,000 feet of film? Did you start with scenes you loved and then go from there?

Yeah, I went through it chronologically, and I was looking at my early notes. And a lot of the things I saw in the early notes are in the film. You’re cutting it down, cutting it down. And a funny thing is that my father, when he was teaching me and helping me with my algebra, said, “Start at the introduction, start at the first page, and just go from there.” So I’m looking at my early notes of “How to Make a Documentary.” That was in my mindset. You don’t know everything. Let me just start at the introduction. And there was even a time when we had no money, and I said to Anne de Marre, “I’ll edit it.” She said, “David, an editor will make it sing.” And she did. She’s a super editor—brilliant—and she’s the one that makes it seamless throughout.

Oh, yeah. Symbiopsychotaxiplasm gave us the license to do whatever we wanted. You wanna have slates in the frame? That’s fine. You wanna have the director giving direction? That’s fine. We had multiple cameras. Why don’t we use it and put them both up there? So the split screens grew out of the license that Symbiopsychotaxiplasm gave us. And then, of course, we had the archival footage, some of which is new, but a lot of this stuff that I had originally shot.

It really captures the overlapping conversations that would have happened in that salon.

Yes, yes, yes.

Well, you know, you can see the reactions. It’s theatrical, if you will. [My dad] said that at the end of it, “The film has to be theatrical and move at a snappy pace.” Which is what we did. Like with Symbiopsychotaxiplasm , you bring all these creative people together, something’s gonna happen. It just grew out of that energy. And they look beautiful on screen.

And the interviews give context to what they’re talking about.

You see the importance of the librarians. Regina Andrews at the library. These guys would come in and she’s fascinated by them. So you have a beautiful young lady fascinated by you and your work, wanting to say, “Hey, do you want to come up to the place? We’re gonna have some people here.”

Oh, absolutely. They were like the nucleus that these folks began to circle around and collaborate. And she says, “You see Langston writing prose, Arna Bontemps doing sketches…” That group contained Arna Bontemps, Langston Hughes, Countee Cullen. So they were critical.

I think about celebrities who are so used to phones and being recorded all the time. Our understanding of how to present ourselves has changed so much with this new reality. When you look back, it does feel like nobody really noticed the cameras. Was that refreshing to watch back?

There were only a couple of instances when the cameras were mentioned. I think when we even put one of them in the film. Ida Mae Cullen said, “Thank you, Bill.” And then one other time when Bruce Newton just said, “Oh… [Gesturing to the camera].” But that was it. It wasn’t like people were like, “The camera’s on now…” They were just interacting and we were just capturing it.

Yeah. It felt almost like a high school reunion.

Yes, yes, yes, absolutely. And the camera people were all experienced with cinema verite. Dad had worked with them for years. I worked with them on camera for years, too, so at that point it’s a matter of having people who are experienced. My father always said, “You can tell a lot about a cameraman if he’s afraid to go in close. That’s where all the action is. You’re all right in there.” And in his interviews on Regina, or on Richard B. Moore, when we recite “If We Must Die” at the end of that—he zoomed in close to catch that, you know?

Yeah.

So the camera people knew what to do. The sound people knew. These are guys we traveled around with all the time. So it’s experienced people with an incredible cast of characters and you bring all that energy together.

Was there a specific moment or interaction that has still stuck with you since you’ve wrapped this project?

My daughter will tell you, and Anne will tell you that. If I had my druthers, Dad would always leave things in the cut long after I knew they had to come out. I’d say to myself, “Why is he leaving it in there?” And the same thing with Richard B. Moore and me. This guy is incredible. You can hear Dad off-camera say, “Give me another magazine. You’re costing me a lot of money, Mr. Moore.” [Laughs] Because it costs money to just put in another 10-minute mag. But Richard Moore is incredible with the history that he knew. And then, of course, there’s Leigh Whipper. There’s another one with his Haile Selassie speech. I love that speech. And he recited it straight through.

At 96.

Yes, 96 years old. He said, “You want to hear it?” And he began. He just bangs it right out. I said that you can’t have the whole thing in, so I cut it down and I said, “What points would Vladimir Zelensky say if he were in the same position?” Then it became kind of easy to cut down, to be honest. “Oh: Alone, without help from the oppressor, a nation leading an army without arms. ” Those were the things that would resonate. I thought people would think of that politically, but the reaction has been like, “Look, he’s still going!” [Laughs]

The other powerful moment for me was the real lament from a few people that the younger generation had forgotten the significance of the people in that room. What did you make of that indictment at that time? Why did your generation struggle to remember these luminaries?

It wasn’t really spoken about. It wasn’t really studied. Students come up to me now and say, “Yeah, I had no idea this existed.” And I think that for us then—they had the Black Arts Movement. It was very much going on at that time. And I was reading a thing from Ishmael Reed. If they had seen the film at that time, they would have said, “Oh, those were revolutionaries. We’re just following their path.” So I think that would have been very illustrative. I think that would have had a big, big effect.

I suppose every generation kind of feels like they’re revolutionaries.

That’s right. “ We’re important. ” Yeah, there was other stuff going on.

When you look back at the salons and dialectics happening at that time, what do you miss most about it?

It reminds me of when I was growing up in my grandmother’s house. People would come over and talk when I was a little kid and you had the bridge parties, smoking, all that. And it took me back. It does remind you of that kind of period, those kinds of interactions. And I think that today, something like this may be happening, could be happening now, but there are no cameras there to record it. So that 50 years from now, people would say, “Oh, yeah, I didn’t know Barry Jenkins was thinking about this.”

There’s two of them—Jean Hutson and Regina Andrews—and needless to say, when they spoke, as Richard Moore says, “Nobody interrupts the librarian.” So they were very much respected, and when they wanted to move people around, they were able to do that.

The New Yorker critic Richard Brody has been a big champion of your dad’s work for years. He wrote that if William Greaves “had been able to complete the movie soon after shooting his footage, it would have literally changed the course of history, and for the better. It would have brought the Harlem Renaissance and its luminaries greater prominence during an era that was neglectful of those movements.”

Right.

What do you make of that idea? Had your generation been able to watch a documentary like this, what impact do you think it would have made ?

I think they would have been more respectful of their predecessors, and I think it would have changed. I’m not going to say “changed the course of history,” but it changed how they thought about themselves. And they would have appreciated and maybe stood up a little straighter and said, “Hey, we are part of something.” I think that would have happened.

I’m sure your dad has been with you in this whole filmmaking process. What did it feel like when this was completed? How do you think he would have felt about this?

I think that he would have said, “That’s my boy. That’s my thing.” I think he would have appreciated the work.

That’s all you want to hear.

That’s all a son wants to hear.

article_text:
An anniversary well worth celebrating, the standard of quality when it comes to the releases of Grasshopper Film is simply unmatched in the world of international cinema. Bringing films by Kleber Mendonça Filho, Hong Sangsoo, Jem Cohen, Albert Serra, Bertrand Bonello, Ryūsuke Hamaguchi, Bi Gan, Pedro Costa, Claire Denis, Alain Gomis, Oliver Laxe, Tsai-ming Liang, Michael Almereyda, Eduardo Williams, and many more to the U.S., the NY-based distributor is now celebrating its 10th anniversary with a special retrospective at Metrograph featuring a selection of standout films. Ahead of the series beginning December 4, we’re pleased to exclusively debut the trailer.

Titles in the series include Afternoons of Solitude, Chronicle of Anna Magdalena Bach, Gueule d’Amour, Kaili Blues, Leviathan, Museum Hours, Nocturama , and The Power of Kangwon Province , featuring a​ Q&A with Jem Cohen for Museum Hours on Friday, December 4 and Q&A with Lucien Castaing-Taylor for Leviathan on Sunday, December 6, with more Q&As to be announced. The series coincides with their release of Kogonada’s zi , which opened in theaters on November 6, as well as the recent release of Kevin Walker and Jack Auen’s Chronovisor earlier this fall.

“Grasshopper was started with two simple beliefs,” said founder Ryan Krivoshey. “First, in films that take risks and approach the world in ways we haven’t seen before. And second, in audiences who share that curiosity, who are eager to discover work that surprises and astonishes, and challenges our ideas of what cinema can be. Over these past 10 years, it’s been incredibly gratifying to see these beliefs affirmed again and again. We’re grateful to everyone who’s come along with us on this journey and excited for what comes next.”

En 2025, Adèle Yon (enseignante en cinéma et cheffe de cuisine) publiait Mon vrai nom est Elisabeth ). Vendu à 282 000 exemplaires (source GFK) et traduit en 21 langues, ce premier roman hybride, entre enquête familiale, essai et récit intime, racontait la trajectoire de l’arrière-grand-mère d’Adèle Yon, dite Betsy, internée pour démence dans les années 1950.

Le best-seller sera adapté au cinéma par Julia Ducournau , lauréate de la Palme d’or en 2021 pour Titane . « J’avais reçu beaucoup de propositions de réalisateurs, mais je ne voulais qu’elle. C’est une artiste fascinante, féministe, indépendante (…) J’ai besoin de passer à d’autres choses, Julia Ducournau va emmener Elisabeth ailleurs », a confié Adèle Yon au Monde , précisant qu’elle ne participerait pas au film.

Polyphonique, hanté par des fantômes et le spectre du patriarcat : tous les ingrédients du livre sont réunis pour que Julia Ducournau fasse de ce récit énigmatique un film (de genre ?) captivant sur les violences intra-familiales et le poids du secret.

Quant à Adèle Yon, elle travaille sur une adaptation théâtrale de son récit, conçue avec Liora Jaccottet, qui sera jouée à partir de février au Théâtre du Rond Point.

Issue

151 Dispatch: Abu Dhabi

The master plan for Saadiyat Island, unveiled at the Emirates Palace in 2007, was presented in the form of a diorama spangled with statement pieces by some of the world’s most celebrated starchitects. Frank Gehry’s Guggenheim loomed with conical silvers and cubic golds. Beside it was Jean Nouvel’s metal dome design for the Louvre. Zaha Hadid had prepared a performing arts center that looked like an intergalactic vessel, neighboring Tadao Ando’s more restrained design for a maritime museum. Foreign press described it as a “cultural Xanadu,” alluding to Kublai Khan’s summer capital or, perhaps with a touch of condescension, to Samuel Taylor Coleridge’s poem of the city as a mythical, idyllic place. The cynicism was perhaps defensible. On Abu Dhabi’s outskirts, Saadiyat was known for its Shaabiyat—a national initiative that distributed single-story houses to Emirati fishermen and their families, replacing the palm-frond huts they had lived in until the 1960s. The area had little more than a small police station, a schoolhouse, and a hospital equipped to administer only first aid.

The capital’s cultural software was also modest. In 2007, neighboring emirates had already entered the global conversation. Sharjah was hosting its eighth biennial with an established museum network. Dubai already had a dozen commercial galleries and was preparing to launch the Gulf Art Fair (later rebranded Art Dubai) and Alserkal Avenue, which overhauled a cluster of Al Quoz warehouses into gallery spaces. The year before, Christie’s had hosted its first Middle Eastern art auction in Dubai. In Abu Dhabi, however, the Cultural Foundation was practically the sole venue for art exhibitions—providing institutional visibility for local artists, but remaining a multipurpose venue.
excerpt_original: Dubai-based art writer Razmig Bedirian traces the trajectory of Abu Dhabi and the master plan for Saadiyat Island, most of which has been realized over the past two decades. Razmig Bedirian

article_text:
One of the more inexplicably popular sources of AI slop today is “Fruit Love Island,” an AI -generated TikTok parody series in which anthropomorphized fruits with abs and cleavage flirt and mingle in 60-second ripoffs of “Love Island.” It is as mind-numbingly dumb as it sounds, and though TikTok started suppressing and demonetizing the videos due to being low quality AI, per the series’ own website blog posts, it persists and has tens of millions of views.

Suffice it to say, your teenager or pre-teen may very well have come across these videos or could easily be obsessed with them. But depending on just how old your teen is, their mileage may vary.

A new study from UCLA and the Center for Scholars and Storytellers called “Rewrite This! How Gen Z and Gen Alpha are Redefining Modern Storytelling” showed that while a majority of young people actually view artificially generated content and stories positively , there is a noticeable shift in how they feel as today’s kids get older.

The study found that 53.8 percent of people between ages 10 and 24 described emotions of either “fascinated” or “excited,” while only 32.1 percent used the phrases “doomed” or “scared.” However, when asked to complete the sentence, “Watching a story with AI in it makes me feel…,” those who felt “doom” compared to “excitement” went up considerably as the survey participants aged up. 27.4 percent of 18-24 year olds used the emotion “doom” compared to just 9.7 percent of those aged 10-13 and 25.1 percent of those 14-18 years old. Nearly half of those between 10-13 felt “excitement” when watching AI content.

The study notes that many of the respondents’ feelings about AI come from AI-native videos they find on their social media feeds. “Fruit Love Island” was one such example, but turns out there are plenty of other examples of AI fruit littering TikTok. It also mentions brainrot memes like “tung tung tung sahur” (no clue) and AI soap operas via vertical, microdramas from ReelShort , DramaBox, Drama Wave, and Pocket Films.

This all feels significant because the narrative tends to be that Hollywood and tech companies are pushing AI even though a lot of people simply hate it and are even repulsed when they see endless amounts of slop on their feeds or in any sort of film or TV. But while the study doesn’t draw any grand conclusions, it suggests there might be a generation gap between Gen Z and the emerging Generation Alpha, who might feel differently and look more favorably at AI than other young people.

“I’d like to see AI portrayed in a balanced and realistic way, showing both its benefits and potential risks,” one 13-year-old polled for the study said. “It would be interesting to see AI helping people solve problems, learn new things, and improve everyday life while also exploring questions about trust, privacy, creativity, and human control.” Smart kid.

This is the fifth year of the study from UCLA and the Center for Scholars and Storytellers. Last year we covered the study with the takeaway that while many young people still love movies and series, many of them are not watching on TVs or in theaters themselves and instead are viewing through YouTube, on phones and laptops, or unconventionally on social media.

This year’s study touched on some of the same questions and found that more than half of young people still ranked “see a movie at the movie theater” as the top weekend activity with their friends if geography and money were not a constraint. But it also had some other new areas of study including what themes they most prefer to see depicted on screen (hopeful messages over partying and drinking), whether they want to see social media influencers in their movies and shows (surprisingly, no), and even if the movies did a good job depicting neurodivergence on screen (only 22.7 percent said “yes, most of the time”).

Find more from the study here .

Films and events

Galas

I Love Boosters

The writer-director behind Sorry to Bother You (LFF 2018) is back with another idiosyncratic, anti-capitalist vision, featuring an all-star cast that includes Keke Palmer, Naomi Ackie, LaKeith Stanfield and Demi Moore.

Screening dates and booking

Check which tickets are still available across the festival – and find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Screening at cinemas around the UK – find out more .

Credits

Director-screenwriter Boots Riley

With Keke Palmer, Demi Moore, Naomi Ackie, Taylour Paige, LaKeith Stanfield

USA 2026. 113min

Courtesy of Universal Pictures

Language English

Certificate BBFC18

Access information

Friday 9 October 21:15

Closed Captions (CC) via WatchWord smart glasses

Thursday 15 October 18:10

Descriptive subtitles

Saturday 17 October 20:45

Descriptive subtitles

Find out about booking access tickets

Introduction

Corvette is an aspiring fashion designer and leader of The Velvet Gang, a group of ‘boosters’ who rob clothes from fashion entrepreneur Christie Smith’s boutiques. But when Smith steals one of Corvette’s designs, The Velvet Gang are pushed to the next level. Boots Riley’s film is a wild fashion fever dream and a rally cry against the system.

Grace Barber-Plentie

Content advice

Contains scenes of drug use, nudity, and sex.

How to book

Tickets start from £10 for all screenings and events in London, with concessions available for many screenings. Booking information and ticket prices .

For non-Members we charge £1 per ticket for online and phone bookings, up to £3 per transaction. There’s no booking fee if you buy tickets at the box office.

If you’re aged 16 to 25, sign up for free to BFI 25 and Under for a chance to get £6 tickets (without booking fees) to all screenings and events, subject to availability.

Missed out?

More tickets may become available for these screenings before and during the festival. Find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Our programmers recommend...

Screen Talk: Naomi Ackie

We welcome Naomi Ackie, who is appearing in I Love Boosters in the festival, to this Screen Talk to discuss her career.

Wicker

Olivia Colman gives yet another bravura performance in this delightfully offbeat comedy, playing an outcast from her village who orders herself a wicker husband.

Klara and the Sun

Oscar winner Taika Waititi’s luminous adaptation of Kazuo Ishiguro’s bestselling novel sees Jenna Ortega play an enthusiastic artificial friend desperate to find a loving home.

article_text:
It is the film everyone seems to be talking about, spawning memes and fuelling feverish online debate about its subject, the disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes.

Now, a month before Nathan Fielder’s documentary You Can See Everything reaches UK cinemas, tickets for screenings are already selling out after its remarkable $15m (£11.3m) opening weekend in the US.

Clare Binns, the creative director of Picturehouse Cinemas, said the excitement was reminiscent of the response to Greta Gerwig’s Barbie, which became a global box-office phenomenon in 2023.

“People are hungry in a way that we haven’t really seen since then,” she said. “And for it to be a three-hour documentary, it’s bonkers.”

Tickets for the film, which opens in the UK on 20 November, went on sale at Picturehouse Central in London before its US opening, Binns said, and demand has prompted the chain to add extra screenings. At the Ritzy in Brixton, the first screen had almost sold out, leading the cinema to sell tickets for a showing at a second.

“It’s fantastic, it proves again that there’s a different kind of audience coming to the cinema,” Binns said. “They came to see Backrooms, they came to see Obsession, they came to see NAZA .

“There’s a real appetite for smart films that talk to an audience differently than the studios have talked to them before. With this documentary, you’ve got a story that has been mined to some extent with the Dropout and podcasts. But I think the fact that Nathan Fielder spent a month with Elizabeth Holmes is a huge draw. He’s a smart guy, and audiences want something they can relate to.”

Cineworld has also reported strong demand. Stuart Crane, its international vice-president of content, said “the speed and scale of demand has been remarkable”.

Initial screenings at Cineworld Leicester Square sold out after tickets went on sale at about 40 cinemas on Sunday. The chain has since added more screenings at Leicester Square and expanded bookings to a further 35 cinemas nationwide.

Vue has reported similar excitement. Dean Cross, its senior screen content manager, said it was “seeing incredible buzz both within the industry and amongst cinemagoers”, and it was “particularly encouraging to see a documentary capturing the attention of younger audiences”.

after newsletter promotion

The momentum for You Can See Everything has been building since it was unveiled at a secret screening at the Telluride film festival in Colorado in September, where audiences were required to surrender their phones. A teaser trailer released the same day quickly went viral, with Holmes herself joining the online conversation, responding to tweets about the film and its trailer.

Co-directed by Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, the film has won widespread critical acclaim. The Guardian described it as “a modern masterpiece of deceit”, praising its unsettling exploration of Holmes and the blurred boundaries between documentary and performance.

Its US opening was the biggest for a documentary in more than 20 years, with more than 2,000 screenings selling out at 855 cinemas. More than 70% of its opening-weekend audience was under 35.

“People want to enjoy films in a cinema with other people,” Binns said. “The younger demographic want shared experiences. They want to talk about it with their friends, and you can’t do that when you’re sitting on your own watching a TV.

“Cinema has been ruled out so many times. Covid, the rise of streamers. Everybody is aware cinema has to change, it has to offer customers something different. But never rule us out.”

Uri Aran, Patricia Ayres, Julie Beaufils, Sedrick Chisom, Carroll Dunham, Nat Faulkner, Sasha Gordon, Kenji Ide, Olivia van Kuiken, Heidi Lau, Jack O’Brien, Kent O’Connor, Trevor Shimizu, Michelle Uckotter

Sep 23 – Nov 14, 2026 Opening Reception: Wednesday, Sep 23, 5pm – 7pm Artist talk led by Matthew Brown begins promptly at 5pm

David Zwirner 5-6/F, H Queen’s 80 Queen’s Road Central Central, Hong Kong Tuesday – Saturday, 11am – 7pm +852 21195900

davidzwirner.com

David Zwirner is pleased to announce a group exhibition organized and conceived by gallerist Matthew Brown that brings together a group of artists who work primarily in the hours of darkness. Nocturnal presents work by Uri Aran, Patricia Ayres, Julie Beaufils, Sedrick Chisom, Carroll Dunham, Nat Faulkner, Sasha Gordon, Kenji Ide, Olivia van Kuiken, Heidi Lau, Jack O’Brien, Kent O’Connor, Trevor Shimizu, and Michelle Uckotter.

Across painting and sculpture, these artists draw upon what fellow nocturnal creative Joan Mitchell called “electric light,” harnessing this visual and temporal state to make works that thrum with the particular energies of darkness and offer an alternative to waking life. For some of the artists on view, nighttime foments periods of creativity and productivity unavailable to them during the day. Olivia van Kuiken observes, “I primarily work at night because it’s the only time when it feels like everyone else turns off. There’s also something about night where I’m less inhibited, less judgmental. I can paint freely without feeling anyone’s eyes on me, let alone my own.” Drawing from lunar cycles, Heidi Lau’s standing sculpture draws on emergent landscapes, its surface forming a hybrid of geological formations and tidal movements shaped by the moon. Suspended above it is a circular ceramic form from Lau’s Moon Jar series, connecting terrestrial and celestial realms.

Others take advantage of night’s oneiric associations, harnessing the power and fantasy of dreamscapes—and still others might make use of the privacy and quiet afforded by these late hours. For Kenji Ide, the nocturnal has become a recurring theme in his sculptures: “The night frequently appears in my work; it is a time when I walk, reflect, and feel truly free. As the movement of society comes to a halt, I feel that my own personal time begins. The darkness and minimal light shift the weight of my mind, allowing me to reach the entrance of an imaginative world. Blurred shapes, with their outlines faded and softened, overflow their boundaries and blend into one another. In such a hazy space, I am able to project and see my own mind.”

The works in Nocturnal call upon the temporal arc from dusk to dawn, exploring how artists have variously invoked its romantic, eerie, eccentric, gloomy, and peaceful aspects. Regarding how the nighttime shifts a setting within a composition, Michelle Uckotter notes, “What is a room but a pinewood box? When we’re left with only artificial light from a bulb or screen, or ambient streetlight coming through a window, it has a way of compressing space into a neat little chamber. Psychological games begin to play out around the shapes in the dark. Just as quickly the narrative dissolves, leaving you alone in a silent room.”
